$$
\begin{aligned}g(x) & =0 \\ 2x-6 & =0 \\ 2x & =6 \\ \frac{2x}{2} & =\frac{6}{2} \\ x & =3\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the function has the single root $x=3.$

questions.worked_solution:
First, we recall the following definitions:

* The global maximum of a function is the highest value that the function attains on its domain. There can only be (at most) one global maximum.

* A global maximum point of a function is a point $(x,y)$ where a function reaches a global maximum. There can be zero, one, or many global maximum points.

For our function, the maximum value reached by the function is $h(x)=5.$ 

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/linear/14209261/assets/70c48ae2f451dfb8194a0f93aaaec406c36d381a8d85d2565320c5a7860351e7.png)

  

Therefore, the global maximum is ${h}_{max}=5.$ The function reaches this value when $x=2,$ so the global maximum point is $(2,5).$

Then, we find the lowest and highest $y$-values in the graph over the domain $x\in [2,4].$

* The lowest $y$ value is $-2.$ This occurs at the point $(2,-2).$

* The highest $y$ value is $2.$ This occurs at the point $(4,2).$

The function covers all the $y$-values between $-2$ and $2,$ including the endpoints.

Therefore, the range is $-2\le y\le 2,$ which can also be written as 

$$
-2\le g(x)\le 2.
$$

questions.worked_solution:
If $r$ is the inverse of $g,$ then 

$$
r(g(x))=x.
$$

To find $r(g(x)),$ we write down the function $r$ and replace every occurrence of $x$ with $g(x):$

$$
\begin{aligned}r(x) & =\frac{1}{2}x+k \\ r(g(x)) & =\frac{1}{2}g(x)+k\end{aligned}
$$

Then, we substitute $g(x)=2x-6$ into the right-hand side of our expression and simplify, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}r(g(x)) & =\frac{1}{2}g(x)+k \\  & =\frac{1}{2}(2x-6)+k \\  & =x-3+k\end{aligned}
$$

However, we know that $r(g(x))=x.$ Equating the expression above with $x$ and solving for $k$ gives

$$
\begin{aligned}r(g(x)) & =x \\ x-3+k & =x \\ \cancel{x}-3+k & =\cancel{x} \\ -3+k & =0 \\ k & =3\end{aligned}
$$
